context.heading: Israel's words for Gentile believers
context.body: Peter calls his readers parepidēmoi of the diaspora: temporary residents among the "scattered". Both were words for Jews living outside the land, yet many of his readers were Gentiles. Abraham called himself "a foreigner and temporary resident" among the Hittites (Genesis 23:4), using the same pair of words in the Greek Old Testament. Peter gives Gentile converts Israel's family story.

context.heading: Tuck up your robe
context.body: "Prepare your minds for action" is literally "gird up the loins of your mind" (anazōnnumi). Men in long robes tucked the hem into their belt before running or hard work. Israel ate the first Passover dressed this way, ready to leave Egypt (Exodus 12:11). Peter asks for a mind hitched up and ready to move.

context.heading: Ransomed from an inherited emptiness
context.body: Lutroō means to set free by paying a price, as when a slave or war captive was bought out. God "redeemed" Israel from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8). Here the captivity is "the empty way of life handed down from your forefathers" (v. 18), the ancestral customs Roman society prized. The price was not silver but Christ's blood, a spotless lamb (v. 19).

theology.title: Father, Spirit and Son in one greeting
theology.body: Verse 2 names all three persons of the Trinity: chosen by the Father's foreknowledge, set apart by the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling with His blood. The sprinkling recalls Sinai, where Israel promised obedience and was sprinkled with covenant blood (Exodus 24:7–8). Salvation is the work of the one triune God.

theology.title: Holy because He is holy
theology.body: "Be holy, because I am holy" (v. 16) quotes God's word to Israel (Leviticus 11:44). Holiness starts with who God is, set apart and pure, not with a rule list. His people are called to reflect His character because they now belong to Him.

theology.title: The story the prophets searched
theology.body: The prophets "searched intently" about the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow (vv. 10–11). The Spirit of Christ was already speaking through them. The Old Testament is not a separate story but the long preface to Jesus, and even angels long to look into it (v. 12).

application.title: Settled too comfortably
application.body: Exiles live in a place without belonging to it. They work, rent, shop and love their neighbors, but they hold it all loosely because home is elsewhere.
application.question: What part of your spending or schedule shows you have settled here as if this were permanent?

application.title: Hope with a target
application.body: Peter says to set your hope "fully" on the grace coming when Jesus is revealed (v. 13). Most of us spread our hope thinly across raises, vacations and other people's opinions.
application.question: If someone looked through your phone, what would they guess you are really hoping in?

context.heading: Milk without the con
context.body: Peter tells readers to put away all dolos, "deceit" (v. 1), and crave milk that is adolos, "pure" or undeceiving (v. 2). The wordplay is deliberate. The milk is logikos, "spiritual" or perhaps "of the word", related to logos. It is the same adjective Paul uses for "reasonable" worship (Romans 12:1).

context.heading: Resident aliens
context.body: Paroikos was a legal category: a foreigner living in a city without full citizen rights. Some scholars think many of Peter's readers really were social outsiders of this kind; most read the word mainly as spiritual identity. Either way, Peter says the church lives as respectful guests whose true citizenship lies elsewhere.

context.heading: Tracing the letters
context.body: Christ left us "an example", hupogrammos, used only here in the New Testament. It described the model letters a child traced over when learning to write. Peter does not ask believers to invent their own response to unjust suffering, but to trace the shape of Jesus' own lines, stroke by stroke.

theology.title: The rejected stone, God's cornerstone
theology.body: Peter weaves Isaiah 28:16, Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 8:14 together. Jesus had applied Psalm 118 to Himself (Mark 12:10). What people threw out, God made the foundation stone of a new temple. Human rejection did not interrupt God's plan; it was part of it.

theology.title: Peter learns Isaiah 53
theology.body: Verses 22–25 quote Isaiah 53: no deceit in His mouth, bearing our sins, by His wounds you are healed, sheep going astray. Peter once rebuked Jesus for speaking of suffering (Mark 8:31–33). Now he calls the crucified Jesus "the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls".

application.title: Honor without agreement
application.body: "Honor the emperor" (v. 17) was written under a ruler who was likely Nero. Honoring a leader does not mean approving every policy, but it rules out contempt.
application.question: Which public figure do you find hardest to speak of with honor, and what would that honor look like?

application.title: Your work as the evidence
application.body: Peter expects outsiders to slander believers but hopes their good deeds will be visible enough to silence the charges (vv. 12, 15). Most people judge the faith by the Christians they work beside.
application.question: If your coworkers judged Christianity only by your last month at work, what would they conclude?

application.title: When the boss is unfair
application.body: Peter speaks to household slaves under harsh masters (v. 18), a world very different from modern employment. The principle still cuts: suffering for doing right, without retaliating, follows Christ's own pattern.
application.question: How do you usually respond when someone with power over you treats you unfairly?

context.heading: A weaker vessel and a co-heir
context.body: Husbands are to honor their wives as the "weaker vessel" (skeuos, a jar or container, often used of the body). Many read it as physical strength or social vulnerability in a world where husbands held legal power. In the same breath Peter calls wives co-heirs of grace, a striking claim then. Christians differ on how these household instructions apply today.

context.heading: Spirits in prison
context.body: Verses 19–20, Christ preaching to "spirits in prison" (phulakē), are read three main ways. Some see Christ preaching through Noah to his generation. Others see the risen Christ announcing victory to fallen angels, as in Jewish traditions about Genesis 6. Others think of a proclamation to the dead. Faithful scholars hold each view.

context.heading: A pledge, not a bath
context.body: Baptism saves "not as removal of dirt from the body" but as an eperōtēma toward God, a pledge or appeal of a good conscience. In later business papers the word described a formal question and answer that sealed an agreement. Christians differ on how baptism relates to salvation, but Peter roots its power in Christ's resurrection.

theology.title: The righteous for the unrighteous
theology.body: Christ "suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God" (v. 18). This is substitution, the heart of Isaiah 53. The goal is not only forgiveness but access: God Himself is the destination of the cross.

theology.title: Patient in Noah's day
theology.body: God "waited patiently in the days of Noah" while the ark was built (v. 20). Few were saved through water, and Peter sees the flood as a pattern for baptism. The same patience still holds back judgment (2 Peter 3:9).

theology.title: Every power under Him
theology.body: The chapter ends with Jesus "at God's right hand, with angels, authorities and powers subject to Him" (v. 22; Psalm 110:1). Believers facing hostile neighbors serve a risen King who outranks every authority that threatens them.

application.title: Ready, not combative
application.body: Peter wants believers ready to explain their hope, but "with gentleness and respect" (v. 15). Winning an argument while losing the person is not what he has in mind.
application.question: If a coworker asked why you have hope, could you answer in two minutes without a lecture?

application.title: The comeback you rehearse
application.body: "Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult" (v. 9). Most retaliation happens in our heads first, as we polish the reply we wish we had given.
application.question: Whose cutting comment are you still rehearsing a comeback to?

context.heading: The flood of excess
context.body: Old friends are surprised believers no longer run with them into "the same flood of reckless living" (anachusis, an outpouring or overflow). Social life in these cities often centered on festivals and trade-guild banquets honoring gods, with sacrifices and heavy drinking. Converts who stayed home looked antisocial, even disloyal, and were slandered for it.

context.heading: A fire meant to test
context.body: Do not be surprised at the purōsis, the "burning" or fiery ordeal (v. 12). The Greek Old Testament uses the word for the furnace that tests silver and gold (Proverbs 27:21). The hostility Peter describes was probably local and social rather than empire-wide persecution, and he treats it as refining, not random.

context.heading: Labeled "Christian"
context.body: Christianos appears only three times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26; 26:28; here). It was probably a label outsiders coined for "Christ's people", and it could be used with contempt. Peter tells believers not to be ashamed of the name, but to glorify God in it.

theology.title: A faithful Creator
theology.body: Sufferers should entrust their souls "to a faithful Creator" (v. 19), the only place the New Testament calls God ktistēs, Creator. The God who made the world keeps His promises in it. Suffering does not mean He has lost control of His creation.

theology.title: Judgment begins at God's house
theology.body: "It is time for judgment to begin with the household of God" (v. 17) echoes the prophets, where God's cleansing starts at His own sanctuary (Ezekiel 9:6; Malachi 3:1–3). God's holiness applies to His people first, and their trials are part of His purifying work.

application.title: When old friends find you strange
application.body: Peter expects a gap to open between believers and old friends who notice they have changed (v. 4). Sometimes the absence of any gap is the more worrying sign.
application.question: What, if anything, do people who knew the old you find strange about how you live now?

application.title: Hospitality without keeping score
application.body: "Offer hospitality to one another without grumbling" (v. 9). Opening your home costs time, food and privacy, and resentment can spoil it quietly.
application.question: When did you last open your home to someone without counting what it cost you?

application.title: Gifts that serve, not shine
application.body: Whoever speaks should speak as one bringing God's words; whoever serves, with the strength God supplies (v. 11). The aim is that God gets the glory, not the gifted person.
application.question: Which of your abilities do you use more to be noticed than to serve?

context.heading: Under the chief Shepherd
context.body: Jesus is the archipoimēn, "chief Shepherd", the head over hired under-shepherds. Peter had been commissioned by Jesus beside the lake to "feed My sheep" (John 21:15–17). Elders do not own the flock; they tend it for its Owner, who will appear and hand out an unfading crown.

context.heading: Your courtroom opponent
context.body: The devil is your antidikos, "adversary", the word for the opposing party in a lawsuit. It fits the Old Testament picture of Satan as accuser (Job 1–2; Zechariah 3:1; Revelation 12:10). Peter pairs the courtroom accuser with a hungry, roaring lion: one slanders, the other devours.

context.heading: Mended like a fisherman's net
context.body: After a little suffering, God will "restore" you (katartizō). The verb was used of mending nets (Mark 1:19), the work Peter once did on Galilee, and of setting broken bones. Peter, who was himself restored after denying Jesus, promises the same repair to weary believers.

theology.title: Under His mighty hand
theology.body: "Humble yourselves under God's mighty hand" (v. 6) uses the language of the exodus, where God brought Israel out "with a mighty hand" (Deuteronomy 26:8). The hand that humbles is the same hand that rescues and will lift up "in due time".

theology.title: The God of all grace
theology.body: God is "the God of all grace, who called you to His eternal glory in Christ" (v. 10). The suffering is "a little while"; the glory is eternal. Peter ends the letter where it began, with grace as the true story believers stand in (v. 12).

application.title: Leading without lording
application.body: Peter warns elders against "lording it over" those in their care (v. 3). The same temptation comes with any authority: a parent, a boss, a team lead, a ministry leader.
application.question: Where are you using authority to get your way rather than to serve the people under it?

application.title: Worry as a control issue
application.body: Peter links humbling yourself with casting your anxiety on God (vv. 6–7). Anxiety often assumes that everything depends on us.
application.question: What worry are you holding onto because letting it go would mean admitting you are not in control?
